strengths: The paper successfully addresses a significant bottleneck in variable-length insertion-based sequence generation: the massive action space and the challenge of identifying a good generation order.

The proposed LFlexMDM model stands on a rigorous mathematical foundation, seamlessly integrating projected discrete flow matching (DFM) with learnable target order dynamics parameterized by Kumaraswamy distributions.

The training pipeline is highly elegant and efficient: it optimizes both the generator and the target rates simultaneously without requiring expensive trajectory simulation, utilizing an autograd-friendly REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator.
The star-graph traversal experiments provide compelling empirical proof of the model's ability to learn task-specific optimal generation orders (generating from endpoints inward to junctions).

On the realistic small molecule generation task (using the SAFE dataset), LFlexMDM demonstrates significant improvements in sample quality and chemical validity compared to the uniform-order baseline (FlexMDM).
weaknesses: The optimization of fully flexible target rates exhibits instability; the authors found that making the unmasking target rate $b_{um}$ trainable destabilizes training, forcing them to freeze $b_{um}=1$ for stability, which reduces the model's theoretical expressivity.

The empirical evaluation is somewhat narrow, focusing mainly on synthetic graphs and molecular generation. Testing on standard discrete text generation benchmarks would help establish the generalizability of the framework to NLP.

The score-based gradient estimator requires generating two latent samples ($k=1,2$) per step to compute the leave-one-out baseline, which increases the forward-pass computational cost during training compared to standard DFM.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant challenge in non-autoregressive and insertion-based sequence generation: learning a globally optimal generation order in a variable-length setting without expensive trajectory simulation.

The mathematical formulation is elegant and rigorous. Parameterizing the target rates via the Kumaraswamy distribution leads to highly tractable, closed-form hazard rates and allows joint training of the generator and order dynamics using a single backward pass.
The proposed LFlexMDM shows strong empirical improvements over the uniform/fixed-order baselines (FlexMDM, MDM, ARM) on both graph traversal and de novo small molecule generation tasks.

The authors conduct a thorough analysis of their design choices, demonstrating why freezing the unmasking schedule ($b_{um} = 1$) stabilizes training and showing how the model successfully recovers locally optimal generation orders (e.g., from leaf nodes to junction in star graphs).
weaknesses: The joint training of both insertion and unmasking rates can be unstable. As shown in Figures 6 and 9, allowing both $b_{in}$ and $b_{um}$ to be trainable causes erratic dynamics and degenerate schedules, requiring the authors to freeze $b_{um} = 1$ to maintain training stability.

The molecular generation experiments, while promising, are conducted on a relatively small evaluation scale (sampling only 1000 molecules unconditionally) and lack comparison with other state-of-the-art molecule generation methods or larger benchmark tasks.
There are some minor presentation and notation inconsistencies in the appendix/hyperparameter sections (e.g., the model is referred to as 'LMFlexMDM' and 'LNFlexMDM' on page 31 instead of LFlexMDM).

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important problem in discrete generative modeling: learning the generation order in variable-length sequence generation models.

Strong theoretical foundation. The authors successfully integrate learnable order dynamics into the Discrete Flow Matching (DFM) framework via an elegant Kumaraswamy parameterization, obtaining closed-form hazard rates and a tractable training objective.

The proposed gradient estimator combining pathwise gradients for the generator and REINFORCE leave-one-out for the target rate model allows efficient joint training in a single backward pass without needing full trajectory simulation.

Impressive empirical results on the star graph traversal task, where LFlexMDM successfully learns the optimal generation order (from leaves to the junction) and dramatically improves the exact match rate on the hard task from 7.4% (FlexMDM) to over 88%.
The method is successfully extended to de novo small molecule generation on the SAFE dataset, demonstrating notable improvements in sample validity and quality.
weaknesses: Training stability issues arise when both unmasking and insertion rates are learned. The authors had to restrict the model by fixing the unmasking target parameter $b_{um} = 1$ to stabilize training, indicating that fully unconstrained joint training of order dynamics remains challenging.

Increased training complexity: Because the REINFORCE leave-one-out estimator requires sampling twice per training step (as shown in Algorithm 1), there is an inherent computational overhead. A quantitative discussion of training time or computational costs compared to standard FlexMDM is missing.

Comparison with other learnable-order methods (e.g., those using Plackett-Luce formulations or other schedule-learning frameworks in discrete diffusion) is somewhat limited, which would help fully contextualize the relative advantages of this DFM-based approach.
